H1268B.emploi: Bérothaï appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 8:8. It is part of the account of King David's military victories over the Aramean kingdoms that threatened Israel. Hadadezer, king of Zobah, was a powerful regional adversary; David defeats him and seizes his wealth and territories. Bérothaï is cited as one of the conquered cities during this major military campaign that consolidates Israel's power and dominance in the Levant.

sens: Man from the tribe of Asher mentioned in the genealogy during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness
H1269.detail: Birzavith is a man belonging to the tribe of Asher, whose name appears only once in the Bible, in the genealogical list of 1 Chronicles 7. He is presented as the son of Malkiel, who is himself the son of Beriah. This name is found in the lineage of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel.
H1269.origine: The name Birzavith literally means "in leanness" or "in thinness," with a possible connotation of "choice" or distinction. The exact meaning remains uncertain, but the structure of the name suggests an image of selection or choice, perhaps related to the olive tree, a symbol of wealth and blessing in Israel.
H1269.emploi: Birzavith appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:31, where he is mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher. This verse lists the descendants of Beriah, and Birzavith is cited as the son of Malkiel. His presence in this genealogical record indicates that he was a known figure of the tribe of Asher during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness, even though no particular event from his life is reported.

sens: Hard and durable metal used for weapons, tools, and construction elements
Ore or raw material from which iron is extracted
Instrument or object made of iron
Chain or fetter made of iron
Strength, hardness, or oppression (figuratively)
Rigorousness or austerity imposed
H1270.detail:
1. Iron is the hard, gray metal that ancient people used to make their weapons, tools, and installations: Tubal-Cain "forged all kinds of tools of bronze and iron" (Genesis 4:22), and Solomon amassed iron to build the Temple (1 Chronicles 29:2). It is a valuable material, replaced by silver in Isaiah's vision of future peace (Isaiah 60:17).
2. The word also refers to the ore extracted from the earth: Job describes how "iron is taken from the dust, and copper is smelted from rock" (Job 28:2).
3. Any object or utensil made of iron falls under this meaning: the locks of the sanctuary "of iron and bronze" (Deuteronomy 33:25), the iron axe (2 Samuel 12:31), or the iron stylus for engraving God's words in stone (Job 19:24).
4. Iron also symbolizes the instrument of captivity: the Israelites are chained "under iron shackles" (Psalms 107:10), an image of slavery and servitude.
5. Figuratively, iron evokes unyielding strength: "You shall break them with a rod of iron" (Psalms 2:9) shows God crushing His enemies. Jeremiah becomes a "forged iron wall" in the face of opposition (Jeremiah 1:18).
6. Iron also expresses imposed rigor: famine and domination are described as iron yokes (Deuteronomy 28:48), weighing on the necks of the rebellious.
H1270.origine: The Hebrew word "barzel" primarily designates the metal itself, with all its properties of hardness and durability. Derived from ancient Semitic roots, it has an equivalent in Aramaic ("parzel"), showing its antiquity in Middle Eastern languages. The image of iron represents solidity, strength, and relentlessness: this is why it easily transitions to figurative use to describe oppression or moral rigor. Isaiah plays on this tension by promising that iron will be replaced by silver in the reign of peace — marking the transition from brute force to beauty and prosperity.
H1270.emploi: The word "barzel" appears about 70 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the historical and prophetic Old Testament. It is used first in the literal sense: raw material (Job 28:2), manufactured object (1 Kings 6:7), or weapon (1 Samuel 17:7). It is also found in relation to elements of worship — the utensils of the Tabernacle — and the structures of the Temple that Solomon carefully prepares. The figurative sense predominates in the Psalms and the Prophets: iron symbolizes God's power (Psalms 2:9), the hardness of the human heart (Isaiah 48:4), or the oppression of captivities. Jeremiah uses iron to describe the prophet's mission: he must be as solid as iron in the face of hostility (Jeremiah 1:18). Famine and slavery are sometimes figuratively depicted as an iron yoke, emphasizing their inevitable harshness.
H1270.portee: For the Christian reader, iron reminds us that God possesses an unyielding strength and a justice that crushes evil: "You shall break them with a rod of iron" speaks of divine judgment. But iron also evokes the rigor that God demands from those He calls — to be as solid as iron in the face of obstacles and doubt, as Jeremiah must be. At the same time, Isaiah's promise — to replace iron with silver — invites hope for a world where brute strength gives way to the beauty and gentle justice of the coming reign of peace.

sens: Chief of the region of Gilead who supported King David
Priest, son-in-law of the first Barzillaï
Israelite father of Adriel
H1271G.detail:
1. Barzillai the Gileadite was a wealthy and aged man of eighty years who lived in Rogelim, in Gilead. When David had to flee Jerusalem to escape the revolt of his son Absalom, Barzillai provided him with valuable assistance: he fed and welcomed him during his stay in Mahanaim (2 Samuel 19:32). After the victory, he accompanied the king across the Jordan, and David offered him hospitality in Jerusalem in reward for his loyalty, but Barzillai refused due to his old age (2 Samuel 19:33-34).
2. There is also a Barzillai who was a priest and son-in-law of the first Barzillai the Gileadite, mentioned as a distinct figure in the genealogy of priests.
3. A third Barzillai was an Israelite from Mahalath, the father of Adriel who married Michal, the daughter of King Saul.
H1271G.origine: The name means "my iron" in Hebrew, composed of "bar" (son) and "zil" (iron). It is a meaningful name that suggests strength and solidity, qualities that the first Barzillai indeed manifested through his unwavering support for King David during a time of crisis.
H1271G.emploi: Barzillai appears seven times in the biblical texts, mainly in 2 Samuel 17 and 19, where he is presented as a chief of Gilead, a wealthy and influential man. His major role is to support David during the flight from Absalom's revolt: he provides food and resources (2 Samuel 17:27), accompanies the king (2 Samuel 19:31), and receives an invitation to Jerusalem in recognition of his loyalty (2 Samuel 19:33). His polite refusal highlights his humility despite his wealth and importance. He is also mentioned in 1 Kings 2:7 when David instructs Solomon to treat Barzillai's descendants favorably in memory of his help. Two other characters with the same name appear in genealogies, one as a priest and the other as the father of Adriel.
H1271G.portee: The story of Barzillai teaches that faithfulness to God and His king can manifest through material help and practical support in times of crisis. His polite refusal of the royal offer also shows that true greatness lies in recognizing one's limits and prioritizing the peace of rest. The recognition that David shows to Barzillai and his household illustrates how God honors those who serve with loyalty.

sens: Man of Israel whose name means 'my iron'
Father of Adriel, who will marry Michal, the daughter of Saul
H1271H.detail:
1. Barzillai is a man of Israel mentioned only once in the Bible. His name, which means 'my iron', evokes solidity and strength. He is known only through his paternity: he is the father of Adriel.
2. Adriel, son of Barzillai, married Michal, the daughter of King Saul. This marriage connects Barzillai to the royal family. Scripture mentions him in 2 Samuel 21:8 specifically to establish this genealogy: Adriel 'of Meholah, son of Barzillai' is the husband of Michal, whose five sons are among those that King David handed over to the Gibeonites for atonement.
H1271H.origine: The name Barzillai comes from Hebrew and literally means 'my iron' (bar = son, zillay = iron), an image of strength and durability. This name reflects the character or nature of the one who bears it in Israelite culture, where iron symbolized solidity and power. Although this Barzillai is distinct from other characters of the same name in the Old Testament (notably the Gileadite who helped David), this isolated mention in 2 Samuel 21:8 identifies him simply by his descent.
H1271H.emploi: Barzillai appears only once in Scripture, in 2 Samuel 21:8. He is mentioned only as the father of Adriel, who married Michal, the daughter of King Saul. This reference is within the context of atonement where David delivers seven descendants of Saul to the Gibeonites. Scripture reports nothing else about his life or actions: he is known only by this genealogical link to the royal house of Saul.

sens: Name of several men, including a Gileadite chief and his descendants
H1271I.detail: Barzillai first refers to a chief of the tribe of Gilead who aided King David. The name then appears in the lists of families returned from Exile: a priest bearing this name married a daughter of another Barzillai, the Gileadite, and the family retained this surname. These passages in Ezra and Nehemiah show how the name was passed down through generations, particularly among the priestly families returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:61 and Nehemiah 7:63).
H1271I.origine: The Hebrew name בַּרְזִלַּי (Barzillai) literally means 'my iron' or 'of iron' — an image of strength and solidity. The root evokes metal, a symbol of firmness and resilience. It is not a flattering nickname, but an assertion of character: the one who bears it is hard as iron, unyielding.
H1271I.emploi: Barzillai primarily appears in the genealogical records of the return from Exile (Ezra and Nehemiah, two books that recount the same event in similar formulations). The name first designates a Gileadite chief contemporary with David, a man of great importance who aided him. Later, his descendants — or at least those who bore this name — distinguished themselves among the priestly families. In Ezra 2:61 and Nehemiah 7:63, we see that a priest from the lineage of Barzillai had married the daughter of another Barzillai, which highlighted the importance of this family. The fact that the text specifically notes this genealogical detail indicates that the name enjoyed a certain notability in restored Israel.

sens: To flee hastily, to leave a place quickly to escape danger or threat
To take flight, to escape collectively or in a group
To be chased, to be put to flight by an enemy force
To pass quickly through a space, to traverse
To run without stopping, to hurry
H1272.detail:
1. To flee hastily means to leave very quickly to escape something threatening. Hagar flees from the face of Sarai who mistreats her (Genesis 16:6), which is a personal and urgent flight in the face of persecution. This is the most direct meaning of the verb: to leave a place quickly because one is in danger or mistreated.
2. To take flight is used when an entire group flees together. Pharaoh learns that the Israelite people have fled (Exodus 14:5), and immediately his heart changes. This is a collective and organized departure, often military.
3. To be put to flight means to be forced to flee by an attack or enemy power. When the king orders his servants to kill the priests, it is because they knew that David was fleeing, in other words, that he was being hunted (1 Samuel 22:17). The verb can also take the meaning of 'to chase', 'to put to flight'.
4. To traverse quickly is a less common but attested meaning. Exodus 26:28 and 36:33 speak of boards that traverse the tabernacle from one side to the other.
5. To run fast, to hurry: Job 9:25 says that days pass faster than a runner, using this verb to express the speed of the passage of time.
H1272.origine: The Hebrew verb בָּרַח (barach) fundamentally expresses the idea of rapid movement and passage. Its root evokes the action of crossing, of passing through, then of fleeing. In Hebrew, there is also the noun בְרִיחָה (brihah) which means 'flight' and the word בְרִיח (briah) which designates a bar or a traverse, showing that the root is related to passage and crossing. In the Psalms and historical narratives, this verb is very common to describe the flights of fugitives and refugees.
H1272.emploi: The verb 'to flee' (barach) appears about 64 times in the Old Testament. It is particularly frequent in historical narratives (1 and 2 Samuel, 1 and 2 Kings) where it describes the flights of kings and warriors. David flees several times from Saul (1 Samuel 19:12, 20:1, 21:10), and David himself is fled from by Absalom (2 Samuel 15:14). The verb also applies to theological situations: the faithful flee before divine judgment (Isaiah 48:20), and Hagar flees from the oppression of Sarai. In the Psalms, the faithful seek refuge in God when they flee from their enemies (Psalms 3:1, 57:1). Jonah flees from the face of the Lord (Jonah 1:3), showing that flight can also be spiritual, an attempt to escape divine calling.
H1272.portee: This verb reminds us that the Bible does not hide moments of panic and flight in the lives of believers. David himself had to flee for his life, which shows us that faith does not eliminate real dangers, but invites us to seek refuge in God. Fleeing can also be a legitimate act: distancing oneself from evil is fleeing temptation (see Nehemiah 6:11). But Jonah warns us that fleeing from God's call is impossible: one cannot escape His will, even by fleeing very far.

sens: Inhabitant of the village of Bahurim
H1273.detail: Barchum designates a man from Bahurim, a small village located on the road that ascends from the Jordan Valley to Jerusalem, near the southern border of the territory of Benjamin. In 2 Samuel 23:31, Azmaveth is presented as 'of Barchum', meaning he is one of the elite warriors of King David, identified by his place of origin.
H1273.origine: The word 'Barchum' comes from Bahurim (בַּחוּרִים), the name of the village from which this man was from. This place name literally means 'the young men' or 'the youths' in Hebrew. The term 'Barchum' is the gentilice form, that is, the one that designates an inhabitant of this village, as one would say 'a Parisian' for someone from Paris.
H1273.emploi: Azmaveth is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:31, where he appears among the 'thirty', the elite warriors of King David. He is identified as coming from Bahurim, which distinguishes him from other warriors in the same list and shows that David surrounded himself with men of value from different regions of Israel.
H1273.portee: This name reminds us that the warriors of King David came from all corners of the territory of Israel, including small villages like Bahurim. This illustrates how God's people were mobilized for the service of the king chosen by the Lord, and how even men from the most modest places could become recognized heroes.

sens: Who has a lot of fat, well-fed, thick
Who is prosperous, abundant, fertile
H1274.detail:
1. The word primarily describes an animal or a person that is fleshy, well-fed, nourished abundantly. It is the concrete image: a fat sheep is a well-fed, plump, robust sheep. Ezekiel 34:20 uses it to contrast the fat sheep (who have been satisfied) with the lean sheep (worn out), in a vision of divine judgment.
2. Figuratively, the word evokes prosperity, abundance, fertility — everything that is "rich," copious, flourishing. A fat pasture is a fertile pasture that well-nourishes the flock.
H1274.origine: The Hebrew root ברה (barâh) evokes the idea of "separating," "creating," or "thickening." The word בִּרְיָה (ber­yah) is phonetically close and denotes the state of being well-fed, plump. In ancient Hebrew, fat was the visible sign of wealth and divine blessing: a fat man was a blessed man, a fat flock was a prosperous flock.
H1274.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 34:20. It is used in the context of prophetic judgment: God condemns the shepherds (spiritual leaders) who have exploited the flock, feeding on the fat sheep while the rest suffer. The opposition between "fat" and "lean" symbolizes inequality and injustice: the powerful enrich themselves while the weak are abandoned. It is a word of moral accusation.
H1274.portee: This word reminds us that in God's eyes, prosperity without justice is condemnable. Luxury and abundance are not inherently bad — they are divine blessings — but they become sin if they rest on exploitation and the neglect of the weak. For the believer, it is a call to justly share the goods received and to care for those who suffer, just as a true shepherd cares for all his flock.

sens: Man of the tribe of Asher during the divided monarchy
H1275.detail: 1. Beri is a man of the tribe of Asher, listed among the descendants of Zophach (1 Chronicles 7:36). His name appears only once in the Bible, in a genealogical list that establishes the lineage of the families of Asher during the time of the divided monarchy.
H1275.origine: The name Beri means "a well" in Hebrew. This name evokes the image of a source of water, a symbol of life and blessing, which was common for biblical names. Although not widely attested, this name reflects the Israelite tradition of giving meaningful names to children.
H1275.emploi: Beri is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:36, in a genealogy of the tribe of Asher. He is presented as one of the sons of Zophach and has several brothers (Suach, Harnépher, Schual, and others). This mention is part of the genealogical census of the families of Asher, compiled probably after the Babylonian exile to establish the identity and continuity of the Israelite tribes.

sens: people or tribe from northern Canaan, mentioned during the time of the Israelite monarchy
H1276.detail: 1. The Bichrites are a group of people or a tribe mentioned in the account of Sheba's revolt against King David. They appear associated with the region of Abel and Beth-Maacah, indicating that they lived in the northern part of the territory of Israel. The name comes from Beri, a man living during the time of the united monarchy, and more specifically from his descendant Sheba.
H1276.origine: The word bichri (בִּכְרִי) designates a human group descended from Beri. The name could mean "from my well" or "of the well," an image that evokes both a source of water and a common ancestor as the source of a lineage. In Hebrew, the names of peoples are often formed by attaching to an ancestor the ending that indicates descent or belonging to a group.
H1276.emploi: The Bichrites appear only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 20:14, during the revolt of Sheba son of Bichri against King David. They are mentioned in association with the city of Abel and Beth-Maacah, two localities in northern Canaan, confirming that this people or tribe occupied the northern part of the territory of Israel during the time of the united monarchy.

sens: Who has a lot of fatty flesh, well-fed
Who is thick or abundant (ears, harvest)
Who is rich, flavorful (food)
Who is prosperous, favored (figurative sense)
H1277.detail:
1. The primary meaning refers to a well-built body, filled with fatty flesh: a fat cow, a fat man (Judges 3:17: Eglon "was a very fat man"). It is a sign of health, good nourishment, prosperity.
2. The word also applies to things: fat ears that bend under the weight of grain (Genesis 41:5: "seven fat and fine ears"), an abundant harvest. The image is one of thickness and fullness.
3. It also qualifies rich and flavorful food, that which nourishes well (1 Kings 4:23: the king's dishes, Daniel 1:15: the young men who eat "the king's delicacies"). "Fat flesh" (Genesis 41:2) literally means "of fat flesh."
4. Figuratively, the word evokes prosperity, abundance, that which is well-supplied and satisfying: the one who is fat has the means to live, he is in ease.
H1277.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of thickness, of fleshy substance. It is related to other forms of the same Semitic family. The basic image is that of a filled, rounded, well-fed body — the opposite of thinness and famine. In biblical Hebrew, "fat" is not pejorative as it can be in modern languages: it is a sign of divine blessing, of a happy and prosperous life.
H1277.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in passages that evoke abundance or prosperity. Pharaoh's dream (Genesis 41) makes central use of it: the seven fat cows and the seven fat ears symbolize the seven years of abundance before the famine. It is also found applied to people (King Eglon in Judges 3:17), to royal food (1 Kings 4:23), and to well-fed animals (Ezekiel 34:3: the shepherds who feed themselves instead of nourishing the flock). Psalms 73:4 and Habakkuk 1:16 use it critically, to describe those who live in opulence far from God.
H1277.portee: This word reminds us that in Scripture, material abundance is a blessing from God. But it also invites discernment: prosperity taken in itself is not the ultimate goal. Pharaoh's dream shows that even the greatest abundance is temporary and fragile. And the critical passages (Psalms, Habakkuk) warn that one who grows fat in forgetfulness of God prepares for ruin. It is a wisdom that calls for gratitude rather than self-satisfaction.

sens: created thing, newly formed
phenomenon never seen before, unprecedented
wonder, marvel that reveals divine intervention
H1278.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to anything created or newly formed, a creation in the strict sense. It is something that did not exist before and has just been made.
2. More specifically, it speaks of a new thing, never before occurred: an unprecedented phenomenon that breaks the usual order. In Numbers 16:30, Moses says that if the earth opens its mouth and swallows the rebels alive, it will be an "unheard thing," because no one has ever seen the earth act this way.
3. By extension, it is a wonder, a marvel that manifests God's creative power and evokes astonishment. It is a sign that God acts in extraordinary ways and disrupts the order of things.
H1278.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to create, to form." It is constructed on the model of action nouns and denotes the result, the created object. The same root, in the first verse of the Bible (Genesis 1:1), expresses the very act of creation of heaven and earth by God. The word thus carries the echo of this primordial creation: it always speaks of a creative action, whether divine or human.
H1278.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Numbers 16:30. This is the moment of the rebellion of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram against Moses and Aaron. Moses, to prove the authority that God has conferred upon him, declares that God will accomplish an "unheard creation": the earth will open to swallow the living rebels. This extraordinary wonder shows that God creates new, unprecedented events, impossible according to the natural order, in order to manifest His will and establish His authority. The context emphasizes that only God can create such wonders.
H1278.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to recognize that God never does anything by chance or according to the mere laws of nature. He creates anew in history, accomplishing wonders that attest to His power and judge those who despise Him. Understanding this term is to remember that God can intervene in totally new and unexpected ways to execute His judgments and His salvation.

sens: prepared food, cooked dish
food given to someone to eat
H1279.detail:
1. The word refers to prepared food or a cooked dish, ready to be consumed. In the account of 2 Samuel 13, Tamar is invited to prepare a dish for her brother Amnon: she makes cakes, which shows that it is about transformed or worked foods, not just raw fruits or grains.
2. More broadly, birya refers to food intended to be given to someone to eat, often in a context of service or care. When David asks Tamar to go prepare a dish for Amnon, it is an act of familial concern or, here, a pretext to bring her closer to him.
H1279.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to create" or "to make." Birya thus carries the idea of shaped, elaborated food, not simply harvested or found. It is food that one "creates" through cooking or preparation.
H1279.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Bible, all in the dramatic passage of 2 Samuel 13, where the false sick man Amnon asks his sister Tamar to come prepare a dish for him. The context shows that it is always carefully prepared food, to the point that Tamar herself must make it. The term emphasizes the intimacy and trust that Amnon feigns to seek — he wants Tamar to bring food from her own hand — in a narrative that will turn tragic.
H1279.portee: This word reminds us of the concrete dimension of hospitality and service in the Bible: to feed someone is to show care and kindness. But here, the story also shows how feigned kindness can hide evil intentions. The dish, initially innocent, becomes the occasion for manipulation.

sens: rigid piece of wood used to assemble or reinforce a structure
lock or bar that closes a door or opening
fortification or obstacle intended to defend a city
figuratively: that which imprisons, holds back, or limits
H1280.detail:
1. In the tabernacle and temples, the bar is a solid piece of wood that spans and holds together the boards of the structure. In Exodus 26:26, Moses is instructed to make "five bars of acacia wood" to assemble the side boards of the tabernacle: it is a load-bearing element, essential to the solidity of God's dwelling.
2. The bar can also close a door or a city. When the Segond speaks of a "lock," it describes the same object — a bar that is slid into rings to block passage. In 1 Samuel 23:7, Saul wants to besiege David in the city of Keilah, which is "provided with gates and bars": the city is thus protected and locked.
3. By extension, the bars represent the defensive strength of an entire city. When Jeremiah 51:30 declares: "The bars of Babylon are broken," it evokes the collapse of its fortifications and military power: the bars have become the symbol of security and dominance.
4. Figuratively, the bar becomes a prison. In Jonah 2:7, the prophet speaks of the "bars of the earth" that confine him: the word then designates the invisible obstacles that hold captive, like the walls of an underground cell.
H1280.origine: The Hebrew word בְּרִיחַ (beriach) comes from a root that evokes the idea of running or fleeing quickly — but the noun has crystallized to designate what precisely stops the flight: a bar that blocks and holds. It is an image in opposition. The word appears in several biblical contexts where structure and solidity matter: in descriptions of worship (tabernacle, temple) and in those of war and city defense. In Exodus and Numbers, it belongs to the technical vocabulary of the sanctuary; in 1 and 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, it describes the fortifications of human cities.
H1280.emploi: The word בְּרִיחַ appears 36 times in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus and Numbers (about 10 occurrences), it is a technical term of the tabernacle: the bars hold the boards. From 1 Samuel onward, especially in the historical books (Kings, Chronicles, Nehemiah), it designates the bars of city gates (Keilah, Gath, Rabbah, Jerusalem after its reconstruction). In poetry (Psalms, Proverbs, Job) and the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Nahum), the word takes on a more figurative and martial hue: broken bars symbolize defeat and enslavement. In Psalms 107:16, the Psalmist celebrates how God "breaks the bars of iron" — the word shifts from the concrete to the divine and spiritual. In Jonah 2:7, it metaphorically designates the confinement of the prophet within the fish.
H1280.portee: This word teaches how the Bible weaves together the material and the spiritual. The bars of the tabernacle remind us that the presence of God requires order and solidity; the bars of cities evoke the importance of defense and boundary. But when God "breaks the bars," it reveals that no human obstacle can withstand His power. For the believer, the bar becomes an image of any limit that only God can cross or break — it is an invitation not to remain confined to the fortress of this world.

sens: a person who flees, who escapes from danger or an enemy
one who seeks to escape, to save themselves
a creature or hostile force that attempts to flee or evade
H1281.detail:
1. The fugitive is a person who flees by abandoning their usual place or state because they are being pursued or threatened. It is one who escapes hastily. In Isaiah 15:5, it refers to the inhabitants of Moab who flee weeping, abandoning everything to save themselves; in Isaiah 43:14, God brings down "all the fugitives" from Babylon, meaning the inhabitants who attempt to escape after defeat.
2. The word can also refer to one who seeks to flee or evade a threat or divine judgment. It evokes the idea of escape, of an attempt to flee. Thus, the leviathan in Isaiah 27:1 is called a "fleeing serpent," not because it literally flees, but because it embodies a hostile force that God will pursue and master.
H1281.origine: The Hebrew word בָּרִיחַ (barich) comes from a root that means "to run" or "to flee quickly." It describes one who is in the act of fleeing. The same root appears in other biblical contexts to evoke the idea of rapid movement or flight. It is a relatively rare word, used to paint the distress and urgency of one who cannot remain in place.
H1281.emploi: The word barich appears four times in the Bible, always in the prophets, and is translated sometimes as "fugitive" and sometimes as "fleeing." In Job 26:13, it qualifies the cosmic serpent that God masters. In Isaiah, it designates both humans fleeing before God's judgment (the Moabites and the Chaldeans) and the powers of evil attempting to escape God's hand (the leviathan). The context is always dramatic: flight, catastrophe, divine judgment. The word emphasizes the helplessness of the one who flees, unable to truly escape God's purpose.
H1281.portee: This word reminds the reader that it is never truly possible to flee from God: those who attempt to flee are always caught or discovered. It invites one to cease fleeing (spiritually or morally) and to turn to God rather than hoping to escape Him, since only His mercy truly offers refuge.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah
Son of Schemaiah
Descendant of the royal family of Judah
H1282.detail: 1. Bariach is a man belonging to the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible, during the account of the genealogy of the kings. 2. He is the son of Schemaiah, who himself is from a royal lineage. 3. He has several brothers: Hattush, Jigeal, Neariah, and Schaphath. He is from the context of the divided monarchy period, when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two.
H1282.origine: The name Bariach means "fleeing" or "fugitive" in Hebrew, evoking the image of one who flees. His father Schemaiah belonged to the royal descent of Judah, which shows that Bariach was part of the noble lineages of the chosen people.
H1282.emploi: Bariach is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:22, in a genealogy of the descendants of David. This passage lists the sons of Schemaiah after the exile, showing how the royal lineage of Judah was perpetuated. His unique appearance in the royal genealogies indicates his importance in the continuity of David's family.

sens: son of Asher, ancestor of a family of Israel
head of a family from which the Beriites descend
H1283G.detail:
1. Beria is a man from the tribe of Asher, one of the twelve sons of Jacob. He first appears in the list of Jacob's descendants who enter Egypt with him (Genesis 46:17). He has three brothers: Jimna, Jischvi, and Jischvi, and one sister: Serach.
2. Beria is the father of two sons: Heber and Malkiel (Genesis 46:17 and 1 Chronicles 7:31). His descendants form a family, the Beriites, which is counted in the desert census along with the other families of Asher (Numbers 26:44-45). His grandsons, Heber and Malkiel, give rise to two other family lines: the Hebrites and the Malkielites.
H1283G.origine: The name Beria (בְּרִיעָה) literally means "with a friend" or "in company." It refers to the idea of bond, brotherhood, or alliance. It is a typical name in the patriarchal context, where names often reflect a circumstance of birth or a blessing.
H1283G.emploi: Beria is mentioned five times in the Bible, always in genealogical lists: twice in Genesis (46:17) during the descent into Egypt, twice in the Book of Numbers (26:44-45) during the desert census, and twice in Chronicles (7:30-31) to recall the genealogy of Asher. These uses show that he is never the subject of a particular narrative, but occupies a fixed place in the history of Asher and his descendants. His importance is genealogical: he represents a link in the chain that unites the patriarch Asher to the twelve tribes of Israel.

sens: Son of Ephraim, from the tribe of Ephraim during the time of Egypt and the desert
H1283H.detail: 1. Beria is a man from the tribe of Ephraim, mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 7:23. His father is Ephraim, son of Joseph, and he has brothers Shuthelah, Becher, Tahan, Ezer, and Elad. He is the father of Sheerah, Rephah, and Resheph. The text reports that Ephraim named him Beria because misfortune was in his house — probably in memory of the death of his two sons Ezer and Elad killed by the men of Gath.
H1283H.origine: The name Beria means "with a friend" or "in friendship." It comes from the Hebrew root that evokes companionship and kindness. This name reflects a positive intention from the father, possibly as a sign of hope or consolation after the tragedies that had struck the family.
H1283H.emploi: Beria appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:23, in the genealogy of the tribe of Ephraim. The passage recounts his birth and the explanation of the name given by his father Ephraim due to the misfortunes that befell his house. It is one of the secondary genealogical names intended to preserve the memory of the ancient families of Israel.
H1283H.portee: The name of Beria and the explanation of its origin remind us that even in moments of sorrow and loss, the fathers of Israel chose names that carried hope and divine friendship. This humble genealogical detail testifies to how the Scriptures preserve the memory of human suffering while maintaining the assurance of God's goodness.

sens: Benjamite during the time of the settlement in Egypt and the Exodus
Head of a family in Ajalon
Father of several sons including Michael and Jishpa
H1283I.detail:
1. Beria is a man from the tribe of Benjamin who lived during the time of Egypt and the desert after the Exodus. He is a descendant of Elpaal and has several brothers and sisters, forming an important lineage of Benjamites.

2. He is known as the head of a family among the inhabitants of Ajalon (1 Chronicles 8:13). With another chief named Shema, he led the inhabitants of this city and participated in military actions against Gath.

3. Beria is the father of nine children, including Michael, Jishpa, and Jocha (1 Chronicles 8:16). These sons maintained the lineage and presence of this Benjamite family in the history of Israel.
H1283I.origine: The name Beria means "with a friend" or "accompanied by a friend." It comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of companionship or association. This name may suggest a birth during a time of blessing or family friendship. There are several characters bearing this name in the Bible: a son of Asher, a son of Ephraim, this Benjamite, and a Levite.
H1283I.emploi: Beria is mentioned twice in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles (8:13 and 8:16), the only passage where he is found. He appears in the context of the genealogical lists of the sons of Benjamin, which served to preserve the memory of families and their legacies after the return from exile. His role as head of a family in Ajalon shows that he was an important figure of his time, responsible for the defense and organization of his urban community.

sens: Levite, son of Shimei, during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness
H1283J.detail: 1. Béria was a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi responsible for the service of the tabernacle and the temple. He is first mentioned during the census of the Levites organized by King David (1 Chronicles 23:10). He was the son of Shimei and had three brothers: Jachath, Zina, and Jeusch. With his brother Jeusch, he did not have many sons, and they formed a single paternal house during the census (1 Chronicles 23:11).
H1283J.origine: The name Béria comes from a Hebrew root meaning "with a friend" or "in friendship." It is a proper name specific to this individual, also borne by other characters in the Old Testament (a son of Asher, a son of Ephraim, and a Benjamite), but the usages provided concern only the Levite son of Shimei.
H1283J.emploi: Béria appears twice in the Holy Scriptures, both in the same passage of the first book of Chronicles (chapters 23:10 and 23:11). These verses list the sons of Shimei during the census of the Levites desired by King David for the organization of temple service. Béria is simply named among his brothers, without any known action or specific role. The text notes that he and his brother Jeusch, having few descendants, had to merge their families into a single administrative unit for cultic service.

sens: family group descended from Beriah, son of Asher
H1284.detail: 1. The Bériites are the members of the family clan descended from Beriah, one of the sons of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. At the time of the census of the Israelites in the wilderness (Numbers 26:44), Moses lists the different families of each tribe: the Jimnites, the Jishvites, and the Bériites thus form the direct descendants of the three main sons of Asher.
H1284.origine: The word comes from Beriah (בְּרִיעָה), the name of a man from the tribe of Asher, whose literal meaning would be "in evil" or "in trouble." The form with the suffix -ites (בְּרִיעִי) is the one given to a family or tribal group to show belonging to a common ancestor: it thus marks the descendants of the same genealogical line.
H1284.emploi: The Bériites are mentioned only once in the Bible, in the passage of the census of the tribes in Numbers 26:44. They are listed among the families of Asher counted with the other descendants of this son of Jacob, at the time when the Israelite people were counting their warriors before entering the Promised Land. It is an element of the genealogical record that shows how the twelve tribes divide into smaller clans, each with its own leader and number of fighters.

sens: solemn agreement between two parties
treaty or pact between nations or leaders
mutual commitment of loyalty
law or ordinance established by a sovereign
pact of friendship or marriage
agreement established by God with His people, accompanied by promises and conditions
H1285.detail:
1. An alliance is primarily a serious and lasting agreement made between two people or two groups. When Abraham and Abimelech shake hands, they make an alliance (Genesis 21:27): they mutually commit to peace and respect.
2. Between nations or leaders, the alliance becomes a political or military treaty sealed by law and mutual promises (Genesis 14:13, where the kings make an alliance to fight together).
3. An alliance can also be a personal promise of lasting loyalty, like that made in a marriage or a trusted friendship.
4. When a king issues laws and ordinances that his subjects must respect, this is also called an alliance: it is a framework established for communal life.
5. Between God and His people, the alliance takes on a unique dimension: God commits to loyalty towards Israel, but also requires obedience and faithfulness. At Sinai, God promises His protection; Israel commits to keeping His commandments (Exodus 24:7-8).
6. This divine alliance bears visible signs and inseparable promises: circumcision for Abraham (Genesis 17:10), the stone tablets of the Decalogue, the worship at the tabernacle (Numbers 10:33).
H1285.origine: The Hebrew word בְּרִית comes from a root that evokes the act of "cutting" or "dividing." An alliance was sealed by cutting an animal in two and passing between its pieces to swear an irrevocable oath (an image still visible in Genesis 15:18). This is why we say "to make an alliance": we "cut" it, we "slice" it so that it is definitive. The word emphasizes the irreversibility of the mutual commitment.
H1285.emploi: The word alliance appears 264 times in the Tanakh, particularly in Genesis (where God establishes alliances with Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob), Exodus, and Deuteronomy (which detail the Sinai alliance). It designates both the pacts between men (Genesis 31:44) and especially the divine alliance, the heart of Israel's religion. Exodus 19:5 and 24:7 show that this alliance has conditions: Israel must obey to receive blessings. Deuteronomy and the prophets emphasize the consequences when Israel transgresses the alliance (2 Kings 18:12, Joshua 7:15): rupture, judgment. But Leviticus 26:45 and Jeremiah 33:25 reveal God's unwavering faithfulness to His alliance despite human unfaithfulness.
H1285.portee: The alliance is the foundation of the relationship between God and His people. It shows that salvation is not an isolated act, but a lasting commitment: God binds Himself to His people forever. It also reveals that obedience to the Word of God is not arbitrary servitude, but a loving response to the commitment of the faithful God. For the Christian, this alliance finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, who seals with His blood the new and eternal alliance (Luke 22:20, 1 Corinthians 11:25).

sens: foreign deity worshiped at Shechem
God of the covenant or pact according to the meaning of the name
H1286.detail:
1. Berith is the name of a pagan god worshiped by the inhabitants of Shechem (Judges 9:46). The temple where he was venerated was called "the house of the god Berith," a sanctuary where people sought refuge in times of danger. This worship reflects the Canaanite religious practices of the time, distinct from the worship of the true God of Israel.
2. The name "Berith" literally means "covenant" or "pact" in Hebrew, suggesting that this god was invoked to seal agreements or protect commitments. It is an ironic or mysterious name for a pagan deity, perhaps linked to rites of protection or promise.
H1286.origine: The word berith (ברית) comes from the Hebrew root that designates a covenant, a contract, or a pact — one of the most important concepts in the Bible. Here, this term is used as a proper name for a Canaanite deity, probably because the worshipers attributed to this god the power to protect alliances or oaths. The context of Shechem, a city in the Old Testament rich in religious history, shows how false gods bore significant names borrowed from religious vocabulary.
H1286.emploi: Berith appears only once in the Bible translated into French (Judges 9:46). It is a deity that the Shechemites worshiped in a fortified temple. After the bloody death of Abimelech and the destruction of Shechem, the people sought refuge with their god Berith, but this refuge did not save them from Abimelech's vengeance. This unique usage illustrates how the Bible mentions the false gods of the nations to show their powerlessness and the absurdity of idolatrous worship.

sens: Alkaline chemical substance used to clean and whiten fabrics
Powerful cleaning agent used in laundry work
Destructive force or intensity (figuratively)
H1287.detail:
1. Potash is an alkaline chemical substance — a white and caustic product — obtained by burning wood or extracting minerals. It was widely used in antiquity to clean and whiten clothing and fabrics, as it dissolves even the most stubborn stains. Jeremiah mentions it alongside nitre (another cleaning agent): even with these powerful products, the people's iniquity cannot be erased (Jeremiah 2:22).
2. By extension, potash refers to the action of deep cleaning, almost purifying by force. Fullers — artisans who washed and finished fabrics — specifically used this potash. Malachi uses it to describe the day of the Lord: "he will be like the fire of the refiner, like the potash of the fullers" (Malachi 3:2), meaning that he will act with a transformative power that purifies but also consumes.
H1287.origine: The Hebrew word בֹּרִית (borit) derives from a root that evokes the idea of burning or reducing to ashes — the burned wood being the primary source of potash. It is a product of fire, which explains why it symbolizes an intense and purifying force. The word appears infrequently in the Bible and remains very concrete, rooted in the domestic and artisanal practices of the ancient world.
H1287.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of cleaning and purification. In Jeremiah 2:22, it represents the impotence of human means against sin: even the strongest potash cannot erase iniquity. In Malachi 3:2, it takes on an eschatological dimension (related to the end times): the fire of divine judgment acts like potash that purifies the sons of Levi, suggesting a total and irresistible purification. In both cases, the word embodies a radical force that cannot be circumvented.
H1287.portee: These two uses remind the Christian reader that the cleansing of sin cannot come from human efforts, no matter how vigorous they may be. Only divine judgment — compared to burning potash — can truly transform and purify. It is a biblical image of the necessity of grace and divine renewal, not of our own merits.

sens: To kneel before someone
To pronounce a word of favor and prosperity upon someone or something
To confer a blessing, to give power or good
To praise, celebrate, give thanks
To be filled with favor, to prosper
H1288.detail:
1. To kneel before someone: The Hebrew word comes from a root that primarily evokes the act of bending the knee. It is the physical gesture of reverence made before one who is recognized as having authority or power. In Genesis 32:26, Jacob refuses to let the angel go until he has blessed him, showing that a blessing is a favor that only one who is above can grant.
2. To pronounce a word of favor and prosperity: To bless is to speak well of someone, to wish and declare their prosperity. In Genesis 1:22, God blesses the animals by saying, "Be fruitful, multiply" — he pronounces a word that activates their reproduction and abundance. It is to invoke or transmit divine blessing.
3. To confer a blessing, to give power or good: A blessing is not just an empty word; it acts. When God blesses someone, he truly produces prosperity. In 2 Samuel 6:12, the Lord "blessed the house of Obed-Edom": his house indeed prospers because of the presence of the ark. The blessing is the action by which God communicates his active favor.
4. To praise, celebrate, give thanks: To bless can also mean to acknowledge God's goodness in words. In Psalm 104:35, the psalmist exclaims, "My soul, bless the Lord!" — he invites to celebrate and thank the Lord for his benefits. It is expressed worship.
5. To be filled with favor, to prosper: To bless in the passive or reflexive form means to receive the blessing, to be happy and prosperous. In Deuteronomy 16:15, the Lord "will bless you in all your harvests and in all the work of your hands" — he will make man happy and fruitful in all his projects.
H1288.origine: The word comes from a root that primarily means "to bend the knee." The transition from this physical image (kneeling) to the spiritual sense (blessing) is explained: one who kneels recognizes the authority of another and receives their favor. In Hebrew, blessing is linked to the transmission of life, strength, and prosperity — a power that passes from the one who blesses to the one who receives. This word resembles the word for "knee" (bérékh). The Aramaic equivalent (bérkakh) has the same meaning.
H1288.emploi: This verb is used 289 times in the Hebrew Bible, very frequently in Genesis where it expresses promises and transmissions of power between patriarchs and between God and man. God blesses creatures (Genesis 1:22: the sea creatures and the birds), God blesses man (Genesis 5:2: Adam), God blesses Abraham and his descendants (Genesis 12:2-3: promise of a great nation). The patriarchs transmit their blessing to their sons (Genesis 27-28: Isaac blesses Jacob and Esau, Jacob blesses his children in Genesis 49). Divine blessing produces visible material prosperity: fertility, wealth, victory. The word is also used to praise God (Psalm 104:35) and, rarely, it can express a veiled curse (Numbers 22-24: Balaam is urged to curse Israel but blesses instead of cursing).
H1288.portee: The blessing reveals that God is neither distant nor indifferent: he personally engages in the life of his people, transmitting his favor and power. For the believer, receiving a blessing is to be assured of God's goodwill, his protection, and his generosity. Blessing God in return is to acknowledge that he is the source of all good and to give him glory. The blessing is one of the most concrete forms of the covenant: God ties his name and power to the destiny of those he chooses.

sens: To pronounce a word of blessing, praise, or recognition towards God
To be blessed, to receive a blessing
To kneel as a sign of respect or prayer
H1289.detail: 1. To bless means to address God with a word of praise, recognition, or blessing. It is to speak well of someone, particularly of God himself, and to acknowledge his goodness, wisdom, or power. Daniel "blessed" the God of heaven after receiving the revelation of the secret (Daniel 2:19), then proclaims: "Blessed be the name of God, forever and ever!" (Daniel 2:20). 2. To be blessed means to receive or be the object of a blessing, to enjoy divine favor. Nebuchadnezzar recognizes that the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego is "blessed" for delivering his servants (Daniel 3:28). 3. The word also evokes the image of kneeling, an ancient gesture that accompanies prayer and the act of blessing: it is to take a posture of humility and respect before God.
H1289.origine: The word comes from an Aramaic root that means "to kneel" or "to bend the knee." This image of the knee bending is connected to the act of blessing: one kneels before God to honor him and address him with praise. The "pael" form (a type of active verbal form) reinforces the idea of an action of blessing given, praised, or proclaimed with intention.
H1289.emploi: The verb "bless" appears 5 times in the Aramaic New Testament (the book of Daniel). It is used exclusively to express praise, recognition, or blessing addressed to God. Daniel blesses God after receiving a revelation (Daniel 2:19), then he solemnly proclaims the blessing of the divine name (Daniel 2:20). Nebuchadnezzar, converted by the miracles, recognizes and blesses the God of Israel (Daniel 3:28 and 4:34). The emphasis is always on the recognition of divine power, wisdom, or mercy in light of God's works in history.
H1289.portee: Blessing God is responding to his goodness and marvelous acts with praise and recognition. For the believer, this verb reminds us that blessing is not primarily a request for favors, but an act of gratitude and worship towards the Lord. It is to acknowledge that God alone deserves honor, and that our mouths should proclaim his glory.

sens: Joint of the lower limb, between the thigh and the leg
Posture of kneeling or prayer
State of physical or moral weakness
H1290.detail:
1. The knee is the part of the human body where the leg bends. It is the joint that allows the lower limb to flex. In Genesis 30:3, a woman gives birth "on the knees" of another, which means she holds her on her knees at the time of delivery, an act that establishes legal paternity.
2. To kneel is to bend the knees, a posture that expresses prayer, worship, or submission. When Solomon kneels "in front of all the assembly of Israel" (2 Chronicles 6:13), he asks God to bless the Temple. Kneeling is not just a physical position: it is an act that shows recognition of the authority of the one being prayed to.
3. The knees can also refer to the state of one who is weakened or afraid: "All knees melt like water" (Ezekiel 7:17) means that terror paralyzes, that the legs can no longer support. "My knees are weak through fasting" (Psalms 109:24) shows that physical or moral suffering takes away strength.
H1290.origine: The Hebrew word בֶּ֫רֶךְ (berekh) primarily refers to the knee joint in the human body. It belongs to a root that expresses the idea of bending or bowing. In biblical Aramaic, the equivalent form is בְּרַךְ (berekh) with the same meaning. The word has taken on figurative meanings: to bend the knee is to acknowledge a higher authority, hence the image of weakness or submission.
H1290.emploi: The word appears 25 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings), the Psalms, and the prophets. Concrete uses dominate: giving birth on the knees (Genesis 30:3, 48:12), kneeling to drink (Judges 7:5), to pray (1 Kings 8:54, 2 Chronicles 6:13), or sitting in the presence of someone important (Ezekiel 47:4). Figurative uses express weakness: knees melting like water in fear (Ezekiel 7:17), knees weakened by fasting or suffering (Psalms 109:24, Isaiah 35:3). The Bible thus strongly links the knee to prayer and the expression of dependence on God.
H1290.portee: For the believer, the knee is a symbol of humility and prayer: bending the knee is to acknowledge that God is above us. This posture is not magical, but it expresses an attitude of the heart. When the Bible says that the knees weaken, it also reminds us that true strength comes from God, not from our own strength.

sens: joint of the leg where it bends
attitude of prayer or submission
H1291.detail:
1. The knee is the joint in the middle of the leg, where it bends. It is the Aramaic word for this part of the body.
2. In the Bible, kneeling is the characteristic gesture of prayer and worship. In Daniel 6:10, the prophet Daniel kneels three times a day to pray to God, expressing through this gesture his respect, humility, and dependence on the Lord. This is why the word "knee" naturally evokes the idea of prayer, supplication, and submission to God.
H1291.origine: This Aramaic word is very close to its Hebrew equivalent (בֶּרֶךְ berèkh, H1290). Aramaic and Hebrew, two related Semitic languages, share much vocabulary. The word simply refers to this joint of the body, but its use in prayer gives it a spiritual significance: to bend the knee is to bow before God.
H1291.emploi: This word appears only once in the Aramaic New Testament, in Daniel 6:10. It is one of the few passages in the Book of Daniel written in Aramaic (rather than Hebrew). Daniel, in exile in Babylon, faithful to his faith despite the king's prohibition, kneels to pray three times a day. This act of prostration is an act of piety and religious defiance: despite the risk, Daniel maintains his worship of the God of Israel by taking the humble and submissive position of the bent knee.
H1291.portee: For the believer, this passage shows that sincere prayer requires a humble posture — not only physically but spiritually. Kneeling symbolizes the surrender of one's own will and the acceptance of God's lordship. Daniel's example invites every reader to regular and courageous prayer, even at the cost of sacrifice, recognizing through his gesture that God alone deserves worship.

sens: father of Elihu, who lived in the time of the patriarchs
H1292.detail: Barakeel is mentioned only as the father of Elihu, the young man who intervenes in the book of Job. His name means "God blesses." He belongs to the family of Ram and comes from the region of Buz (Job 32:2). Although Barakeel himself never speaks in the Bible, his son Elihu speaks up to contest the words of Job and his three friends (Job 32:6).
H1292.origine: The name Barakeel combines two Hebrew elements: "barak" (to bless) and "El" (God). It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that incorporates the divine name to express a blessing or a divine quality: "God blesses."
H1292.emploi: Barakeel is mentioned twice in the Bible, both times in the book of Job, in chapter 32. These two occurrences serve only to identify Elihu as his son and to establish his genealogical origin (from the family of Ram, from Buz). Elihu, the son of Barakeel, is an enigmatic character in the book of Job: he is not counted among the three friends who converse with Job, but he speaks up after the others have finished talking, young and long silent before expressing his indignation.

sens: Action of blessing, word that calls good upon someone
What makes happy and prosperous, advantage received from God
Praise, act of thanksgiving to God
Gift, present offered to someone
Agreement of peace, treaty between enemies
H1293.detail:
1. The blessing is primarily the act of blessing: it is a word spoken to invoke good upon someone. God blesses Abraham and promises him a great offspring (Genesis 12:2), and Jacob blesses his sons before dying, passing on the blessings of his ancestors (Genesis 49:26). It is an effective power: to speak well is to do good.
2. The blessing also refers to the result of this action: prosperity, wealth, everything that makes life happy. When Israel obeys God, blessings pour out upon him like rain: abundance, health, victory (Deuteronomy 28:2). It is the tangible favor of God.
3. It can also be a praise, an act of thanksgiving addressed to God for his benefits. Nehemiah calls to bless the Lord, to celebrate his greatness (Nehemiah 9:5).
4. The word can also refer to a gift, a present: David sends spoils as a "gift" to the elders of Judah (1 Samuel 30:26).
5. Rarely, a blessing is an agreement, a peace: a kind of mutual gift sealing reconciliation.
H1293.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to bend the knee," "to kneel," as before a king or a god. The blessing is therefore a gesture of honor and submission that accompanies the word of good. This is why to bless is to recognize the greatness of the one being blessed and to wish him prosperity. The same root forms the word "bless" (verb) and other words in the family of good and favor.
H1293.emploi: This word appears 64 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Torah (Genesis, Deuteronomy), the Psalms, and Proverbs. It constantly recurs in the teaching on God's covenant: obeying God brings blessings, disobeying pushes them away (Deuteronomy 11:26-27, 28:2, 30:19). Proverbs uses it to say that the blessing rests on the righteous, on the one who is generous and merciful (Proverbs 10:6, 11:25). David asks that God continue his blessing on his house (2 Samuel 7:29). The context remains very concrete: the blessing visibly produces good, wealth, and peace.
H1293.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God does not merely command: he blesses those who obey him. The blessing is not just an empty word; it is a force that acts. It invites the reader to seek God's favor through obedience and righteousness, and to recognize that all good comes from him. It also shows that blessing others is participating in God's action that does good.

sens: Benjaminite warrior in the service of King David
H1294G.detail: Beraca is a military leader from the tribe of Benjamin who rallied to David during his reign. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, listed among the valiant warriors who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12:3), alongside other leaders like Achiezer and Joash.
H1294G.origine: The name Beraca means "blessing" in Hebrew, derived from the root "brk" which expresses the idea of blessing and prosperity. It is a common theophoric name in the Old Testament, reflecting the hope that this child would be a blessing to his family.
H1294G.emploi: Beraca appears only once in the Scriptures (1 Chronicles 12:3). He is cited as one of the valiant warriors who gathered around David at Ziklag during the time when David was fleeing from King Saul. This list of warriors illustrates the military support that David enjoyed before becoming king of Israel.

sens: Valley of the wilderness of Judah, near Tekoa
Place of assembly and blessing
H1294H.detail: Beraca is a valley located in the wilderness near Tekoa, in Judah. It is here that King Jehoshaphat and the people gathered after the miraculous victory over the Moabite armies, to bless the Lord and give thanks (2 Chronicles 20:26). The very name of the place perpetuates this memory: the Israelites called it "valley of Beraca" — literally "valley of Blessing" — because they had blessed God together there; this name has remained until the time the account was written.
H1294H.origine: The Hebrew word berakhah means "blessing": it is the same root that designates the act of blessing, of asking God to pour out His favors. Jehoshaphat and his people gave this valley a memorial name, transforming a desolate place into a sanctuary of gratitude towards God. This is a biblical example where a place name carries a spiritual message within itself.
H1294H.emploi: The valley of Beraca appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 20:26. It is the setting for a decisive moment: after God delivered Jehoshaphat and his army from the invasion of the Moabites and Ammonites, the people gather in this valley to publicly confess the power and goodness of the Lord. It is a place consecrated by collective thanksgiving, and the text emphasizes that the memory of this name has passed through generations until the time of the writing of the book.
H1294H.portee: The valley of Beraca teaches us that God transforms places of deliverance into places of memory. When God acts for His people, they honor His name and create monuments — even a simple valley name — so that future generations remember His wonders and share their gratitude. It is an invitation to recognize God's acts in our own lives and to bear witness to them.

sens: Large area of stagnant water, smaller than a lake
Water reservoir constructed for the needs of a city or a king
H1295G.detail:
1. A pond is a large body of water that does not flow, unlike a river or stream: it is still and deep water. In Nehemiah 2:14, it refers to "the king's pool," meaning a basin built to store water in Jerusalem, likely to supply the city or irrigate royal gardens.
2. This word often designates a hydraulic structure — not just a natural body of water. Nehemiah, inspecting the walls of Jerusalem, passes specifically through the area of this king's pool, which was large enough for the ground to have become muddy and difficult to traverse on horseback.
H1295G.origine: The Hebrew word בְּרֵכָה (berekah) is related to a root meaning "to kneel" or "to bend," hence the image of a depression in the ground where water accumulates and "kneels." It is a common feminine noun. The expression "the pool of Shelah" in the biblical text combines this word with Shelah (שֶׁ֫לַח), likely designating the source or basin located near the eastern sector of Jerusalem, in the Kidron Valley.
H1295G.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible in the sense of a water basin. Nehemiah 2:14 mentions it during the inspection of the walls of Jerusalem after the exile: Nehemiah goes around the city and passes near "the gate of the fountain and the king's pool." This pool was a known royal installation, likely from the time of the kings of Judah before the destruction of 586 B.C., and still existing in Nehemiah's time (5th century B.C.). The context shows a specific, identifiable place near a gate of Jerusalem.
H1295G.portee: This passage shows us Nehemiah as a man of action who methodically inspects the ruins of Jerusalem to assess the extent of the reconstruction work. The king's pool reminds us that Jerusalem was an organized city, with water supply infrastructures — a constant concern in a semi-arid land. This illustrates the historical and geographical reality of Nehemiah's work: to rebuild a city is also to restore its essential services.

sens: Basin of stagnant water, natural or dug
Water reservoir for irrigation or water supply
Comparative term to describe beauty or clarity
H1295H.detail:
1. A pond is a basin of water that does not flow, either formed naturally or dug by man. It is distinct from a river or stream. At Gibeon, it was a meeting place where the men of Joab and those of David stopped (2 Samuel 2:13).
2. In cities, ponds were dug to create water reserves, useful in case of siege or drought. Hezekiah built a pool and an aqueduct to bring water to Jerusalem (2 Kings 20:20), and Isaiah speaks of the lower pool of the city of David, intentionally retained during a military threat (Isaiah 22:9).
3. In poetry, the pond becomes an image of clarity and depth: the eyes of the beloved in the Song of Songs are compared to the pools of Heshbon, evoking clear and beautiful water (Song of Songs 7:5).
H1295H.origine: The Hebrew word בְּרֵכָה (berekha) comes from the root ברך (B-R-K), which carries the idea of "to bend," "to curve." A pond is a depression in the ground where water accumulates and remains. This word has variants in neighboring Semitic languages. In biblical Greek, the term κολυμβήθρα (kolumbèthra) is also found, which designates a basin or water reservoir.
H1295H.emploi: The word "pond" appears 14 times in the provided biblical usages, primarily in historical narratives and descriptions of Jerusalem. It first designates real places: the pond of Gibeon (2 Samuel 2:13), the pond of Samaria where King Ahab's chariot was washed (1 Kings 22:38), and the water reservoirs of Jerusalem built or protected throughout history. In urban texts (2 Kings, Nehemiah, Isaiah), they are strategic installations meant to supply the city. In the Song of Songs (7:5), the word takes on a figurative and poetic sense, an image of beauty and clarity. This semantic richness shows that the pond could be a practical concern or a symbol of splendor.
H1295H.portee: The pond reminds us of the importance of water in the lives of biblical peoples: it is a vital resource that is protected and of which one is proud. For the believer, it also symbolizes accumulation and reserve, the wisdom of keeping what nourishes. In the Song, being able to recognize beauty in what is simple and useful — like a pond — invites us to see God's glory in ordinary creation.

sens: son of Zerubbabel, a man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H1296G.detail: Bérékia is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 3:20, where he appears as one of the five sons of Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah who led the return from Babylonian exile. His name appears in the royal genealogy of Judah, establishing the line of descent after the destruction of Solomon's temple.
H1296G.origine: The name Bérékia means "Jehovah blesses" in Hebrew. It is composed of "Berekh" (to bless) and "Yah" (Jehovah), two common theophoric elements in Hebrew names. This type of name expresses the family's trust in divine blessing, particularly appropriate for a man from the royal family restored after the exile.
H1296G.emploi: Bérékia is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:20, in the genealogical list of the sons of Zerubbabel. He is one of five listed in the order: Haschuba, Ohel, Bérékia, Hasadia, and Juschab-Hésed. His presence in the genealogy of the kings confirms his belonging to the family of David and his role in the restoration of Judah after the exile.

sens: Levite, father of the singer Asaph
Porter of the ark of the covenant
H1296H.detail:
1. Bérékia is a Levite from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is best known as the father of the singer Asaph, who played an important role in the temple services and the praise of God's people (1 Chronicles 6:39). He belonged to the tribe of Levi, dedicated to the service of God in the sanctuary.
2. Bérékia is also mentioned as the porter of the ark of the covenant (1 Chronicles 15:23), meaning he had the responsibility of guarding and overseeing this sacred symbol of God's presence among Israel.
H1296H.origine: The name Bérékia means "God blesses" or "God blesses" (from the root "barak" which means to bless). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name, which was common among Levites and temple servants. This name reflects the parents' trust in divine blessing upon their child.
H1296H.emploi: Bérékia is mentioned three times in Chronicles, always in connection with worship and praise in Jerusalem. He is first presented as the father of the musician Asaph (1 Chronicles 6:39 and 15:17), one of the three main leaders of the singers under King David. He is then cited as the porter of the ark (1 Chronicles 15:23), a prestigious role reserved for trustworthy Levites. These mentions show that Bérékia belonged to an important Levitical family, invested in divine service and sacred music.

sens: Member of the tribe of Levi at the time of the Return from Exile
The name means "God blesses"
H1296I.detail: Bérékia is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:16, where he is presented as the son of Asa and the father of several important descendants. His name carries a prophetic significance: it expresses God's blessing, a promise particularly meaningful for a member of the priestly tribe restored after the Exile.
H1296I.origine: The name Bérékia comes from the Hebrew "barak" (to bless) and "Yah" (the Lord). It literally means "Jehovah blesses" or "God blesses." It is a typical theophoric name of the Old Testament, where a person's name proclaims a truth about God and His actions. The root "barak" expresses divine blessing, the transmission of life and prosperity.
H1296I.emploi: Bérékia appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 9:16. He is presented as a Levite who lived in the villages of the Nethophathites after the Return from Exile. Although his mention is brief, his lineage is significant: he is the son of Asa and belongs to a line of important Levites. The genealogy in which he appears shows the organization of worship and temple services during the restoration of Israel after the Babylonian Exile.
H1296I.portee: This Levite represents the continuity of God's covenant with His people even after the Exile. His name, "God blesses," reminds us that divine blessing persists beyond punishment and captivity. For the Christian reader, Bérékia embodies God's restoration and faithfulness: even in trials, His promises remain.

sens: Ephraimite leader during the reign of King Ahaz
Son of Meschillémoth
H1296J.detail: Bérékia is a leader from the tribe of Ephraim who lived during the reign of King Ahaz, during the period of the divided monarchy. His only mention in the Bible is found in 2 Chronicles 28:12, where he appears alongside other Ephraimite leaders, including Azariah and Hezekiah. These men, all sons of prominent figures (Bérékia being the son of Meschillémoth), rose up to oppose the soldiers returning from a military campaign, showing that they exercised moral and political authority in their community.
H1296J.origine: The name Bérékia means "Jehovah blesses" in Hebrew, composed of "berekh" (blessing, knee) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name). This theophoric name expresses trust in divine blessing. Although this Bérékia is mentioned only once, several other figures bear the same name in the Old Testament, including a Levite who returned from exile and the father of the prophet Zechariah.
H1296J.emploi: Bérékia, son of Meschillémoth, is an Ephraimite leader mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 28:12. He intervenes during the reign of King Ahaz, when the army of Judah returns from Syria and the Northern Kingdom after a battle. Alongside other renowned Ephraimite leaders, he refuses to allow the prisoners of war and the spoils to be brought to Jerusalem, thus demonstrating a moral conscience and decision-making power within the community structures of Ephraim.

sens: Man of Judah at the time of the return from exile
Father of Meschullam, a leader who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem
H1296K.detail: Bérékia is a minor character in the Bible mentioned in the book of Nehemiah at the time of the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the exile. He is the father of Meschullam, who was one of the key leaders in this reconstruction (Nehemiah 3:4). His name means "God blesses" or "the Lord blesses." He also appears in the family alliances of that time: his son Jochanan married the daughter of another Meschullam, showing how prominent families were linked together (Nehemiah 6:18).
H1296K.origine: The name Bérékia comes from the Hebrew berakh (to bless) and Yah (God). It literally means "God blesses" or "the Lord blesses." It is a common compound name in the Old Testament, where divine blessing is directly expressed in a person's name, marking an expectation or trust in God's protection and favor.
H1296K.emploi: Bérékia is mentioned three times in the book of Nehemiah, all during the time when Jerusalem is being rebuilt after the exile (around 444 B.C.). He is first presented as the father of Meschullam, one of the main leaders of the wall reconstruction efforts (Nehemiah 3:4, 3:30). These references show that he belonged to an influential family of Judah that played a key role in the restoration of the city. He finally appears in the context of marital alliances of the period (Nehemiah 6:18), revealing the political and social importance of his lineage.

sens: father of the prophet Zechariah
man from the Levitical priestly lineage
H1296L.detail:
1. Berekiah is the father of the prophet Zechariah, to whom God speaks during the time of exile and the return to Jerusalem. This is how he is primarily known: Zechariah 1:1 presents him as "Zechariah, son of Berekiah, son of Iddo," clearly establishing his place in this prophetic genealogy.
2. Berekiah belongs to a family of Levites, the tribe dedicated to the service of the temple. This context explains why God entrusts his descendants — notably his son Zechariah — with a major prophetic mission at the critical moment of the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the exile.
H1296L.origine: The Hebrew name Berekiah literally means "The Lord blesses" or "Jehovah blesses" (berekh = blessing, and Yah = God). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the divine name within it, which was common among pious families in Israel. This name expresses an act of faith or a supplication: the parents confess that God blesses, or they ask for His blessing.
H1296L.emploi: Berekiah appears twice in the Bible, both times in the book of Zechariah (Zechariah 1:1 and 1:7), each time to identify the father of the prophet Zechariah. No other details about his life are given in the texts. However, according to Hebrew tradition reported in ancient commentaries, several men bore this name in the history of Israel: a son of Zerubbabel (who governed after the exile), Levites who participated in the return from exile and the reconstruction of the temple, and a chief of Ephraim during the reign of King Ahaz. The Bible itself does not specify whether this Berekiah is one of these other figures or a distinct individual.
H1296L.portee: The name Berekiah reminds us that God's promises are fulfilled through pious generations. By giving the prophecy to Zechariah, son of Berekiah, God honors a lineage devoted to His service. For the Christian reader, this illustrates how God chooses and blesses the descendants of those who fear Him and call upon Him in faith.

sens: Conjunction marking opposition or restriction between two ideas
Expresses a concession: despite what has just been said, here is what remains true
Introduces an exception or contrast with what precedes
H1297.detail:
1. Conjunction of opposition. It connects two contrary or incompatible ideas: the first states something, the second contradicts or nuances it. For example, in Daniel 2:28, the king asked his wise men to interpret his dream, but they could not; "but" marks the turning point: "there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets."
2. Conjunction of restriction or concession. It allows for maintaining an idea despite an objection or limitation. In Daniel 4:15 and 4:23, an angel orders the tree of Nebuchadnezzar to be cut down, "but" the tree will remain partially alive: its roots will survive underground. The contrast concerns the partial destruction.
3. Conjunction of exception or reaffirmation. It introduces what remains true or valid despite the circumstances. In Daniel 5:17, Daniel refuses the king's gifts, "nevertheless" he will read the writing and give its interpretation: his commitment persists despite the refusal of the gifts. In Ezra 5:13, the work was interrupted, "however" it is in the first year of Cyrus that the orders for reconstruction came.
H1297.origine: This conjunction from biblical Aramaic comes from the Semitic family of words of restriction and limitation. It mainly appears in the Aramaic sections of Daniel and in the book of Ezra (chapters 4–6), reflecting the official language of the Babylonian and Persian empires. It functions as a logical marker to create contrast and narrative tension between two statements.
H1297.emploi: The word appears five times, exclusively in the Aramaic passages of the Old Testament: three times in Daniel (chapters 2, 4, 5) and once each in Ezra and Daniel. In all cases, it marks a decisive articulation of the narrative: it introduces what overturns a difficult situation or corrects a statement. In Daniel 2:28, it announces that God can where the wise men have failed. In Daniel 4:15 and 4:23 (the same scene reported twice), it tempers a sentence of destruction. In Daniel 5:17 and Ezra 5:13, it maintains a promise or action despite contrary appearances. It is a tool of divine revelation: God intervenes "but," that is, despite what the previous situation seemed to indicate.
H1297.portee: This conjunction teaches the reader that God has the final word. Each time it appears, it emphasizes how the Lord breaks through obstacles, persists in His purposes, and overturns appearances. It invites the believer to recognize, in moments of impasse or apparent defeat, that God always says "but": there is a continuation, a grace, an outcome that human wisdom had not foreseen.

sens: King of Sodom during the time of the Patriarchs
H1298.detail: Bera is the king of Sodom mentioned only once in the Bible, during the account of the war of the four kings against the kings of the Pentapolis (Genesis 14:2). His name means "son of evil" in Hebrew, which likely reflects the wicked character of Sodom, a city famous for its sins.
H1298.origine: The name Bera is formed from two Hebrew elements: "ben" (son) and "ra" (evil, bad). This onomastic composition evokes the moral identity of the one who bears this name and of his people — a common practice in the Old Testament where personal names reflect character traits or spiritual realities. Sodom itself symbolizes in the rest of the Bible divine judgment against sin.
H1298.emploi: Bera appears only once in the Scriptures, in Genesis 14:2, where he is presented as king of Sodom. He is named alongside the other kings defeated by the four kings from the North (Chedorlaomer and his allies). This battle precedes shortly the destruction of Sodom in Genesis 19, which gives the character a place in the history of divine judgment on this sinful city. His sole mention underscores his local historical importance rather than his relevance in the biblical plan of salvation.

sens: To burst forth suddenly producing bright light, like lightning
To deploy or launch flashes of light dazzlingly
H1299.detail:
1. The word describes the spectacular natural phenomenon of lightning that crosses the sky in an instant: an intense and fleeting glow that bursts forth and captivates the eye. In Psalm 144:6, the psalmist prays to God to "shine" the lightning (that is, to launch it) to defeat his enemies, using the image of these celestial luminous manifestations as a sign of divine power.
2. More broadly, the verb evokes the action of deploying or sending lightning, as a weapon or instrument of divine will: it is God who "shines" or launches the lightning from heaven to strike, illuminate, or manifest His greatness.
H1299.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "shining" and "radiating." It evokes the sudden and intense visual phenomenon: the root is related to the noun "lightning" and describes the dynamic action of this light that bursts forth. Several images of lightning associated with divine power and presence are found in the Old Testament.
H1299.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 144:6, where the psalmist asks God to shine the lightning. The context is that of a warrior's prayer: the believer invokes divine help against his enemies by asking God to deploy His heavenly power, symbolized by the lightning that "shines" and illuminates the sky. This image expresses the conviction that God controls the forces of nature and uses them to accomplish His will and protect His people.
H1299.portee: This word reminds us that in biblical thought, natural phenomena — lightning, thunder, storms — are never accidents or purely physical phenomena: they are signs of God's action and power. By praying this way, the believer acknowledges that God alone commands the celestial forces and asks for the direct intervention of the Lord in spiritual and practical battles. It is an invitation to see in the powers of nature a manifestation of divinity and God's sovereign control.
